The kernel is clean with no active edits, and 203 cut Let answers are available. To compare heads fairly, I need loops that really are periodic at token level, so I'll pick by a mechanical rule. An answer qualifies if its last 150 tokens all match at some lag P, the loop starts late enough to leave pre-loop tokens as a control, and it runs at least 200 tokens. From those I'll take four that span short to long periods, without choosing by reading the text.

Each of the two texts will hold two prompt-and-answer pairs, so one pass covers four loops, and I'm storing exact token positions for the period, onset and answer start. Second turns do see the earlier turn in context, which is a small distortion, but it doesn't change which token a head would need to copy. The notes get the exact plan before the pass.

Nearly all the cut Let answers qualify (189 of 203), so these loops are exact at token level, which makes a copying mechanism more plausible. The four picks span periods of 16, 45, 79 and 143 tokens, each with a real pre-loop stretch, and both texts fit within the limit. The positions and the plan are saved.

Now the attention pass on the original model. The decision test was set beforehand: a head that locks onto the copy position justifies a removal test in generation, and spread-out attention closes the loop line for good.

The attention arrays are in: the 1,682-token texts cover all four loops, and their mean token logprob of about -0.4 shows the model is highly confident inside them. Now the head-level measure.

For every in-loop token I'll compute, per head, the attention landing on the matching positions in earlier repetitions: the token to be copied next, and the same token again. Two controls will keep this honest: nearby off-target positions in the loop, and the same lag before the loop starts. A real copy head should have far more attention on target than either control, consistently across all four loops, with periods from 16 to 143. If several heads share modest amounts, or only one loop shows the effect, there's no copy circuit to remove. I'm also reporting attention to the problem during loops, because if heads have abandoned the prompt entirely, that's a different finding worth having.

This is a sharp result, and the most specific component I've found for the loops. Inside a loop, six heads lock onto the next token to copy from earlier repetitions: L5 h2 (.452), L17 h3 (.401), L17 h2 (.390), L17 h0 (.386), L5 h3 (.314) and L11 h1 (.287). Off-target positions get only about .003, a ratio of 100x or more, and L23 takes no part. Pre-loop attention at the same lag is .03-.07, and the lock-on shows in all four loops, though unevenly: L5 h3 ranges from .757 at the shortest period down to .091.

The important catch is that these are largely the heads I already identified for retrieval: L17 h0, L5 h2, L17 h3 and L11 h1 for reading numbers, and L17 h2 and h3 for operands. So looping isn't a separate circuit. It's the model's normal pointer-copy mechanism aimed at its own text. Simply removing all of them would damage retrieval, as E11b showed, so I need to find out which heads the loops depend on most and which legitimate work depends on least. L5 h3 has no known retrieval role, so it's the natural first candidate.

A teacher-forced screen is the efficient way to do this. I'll build one fixed text set of own DEV answers: all exactly periodic loops, plus correct and wrong finished answers as controls. For each candidate edit, the question is how often the model's top choice departs from the copied token during the first repetition (an escape from the loop), compared with how often it departs from a correct answer's own tokens (collateral damage). A useful edit would have a high escape rate and low damage. If they rise together, loops can't be separated from legitimate copying, and the line closes. This block builds the set and records the plan, and the baseline pass on the original model comes next.
